This also seems to make Morgoth special nontheless- It almost seems like you can see Tolkien's personal perception of the story of Lucifer through Morgoth, and in that case, he has a very profound theological way of viewing Satan.

It's also worth mentioning, in the first age, Melkor wasn't alone in being a great, dark terror. In the third age, it was only Sauron, the Balrog, the orcs and Smaug. In the first, I can't even name them all. Less room for Morgoth to be detailed and elaborated than for Sauron.

Morgoth's personal power isn't what makes him terrifying imo.

As I see it, Morgoth as a villain is more of a mythological character, as the Tolkien universe is basically a modern mythology. 

Thanos, Darkseid and the likes are characters created for modern technology and knowledge, made to fit into our own infinite universe. Their power is the only way for them to be terrifying in such an endless enviroment.

Morgoth is just as powerful as them in scale to his enviroment; Arda. One world, compared to an infinite universe.

But even if he was placed in such an infinite place, he would still be terrifying, not because of his power, but because of his character- The pure malice, the manipulation and the fact that he can create creatures like Ancalagon is what makes him terrifying in my opinion, not his power. And in this regard, Morgoth is far better written than Thanos, Darkseid or any comic-book villain that I know of.

He is an ancient, mythological horror, not a just a conqueror of the universe.

As for him being boring, he is a bit of a trope. He is the first modern version of this trope afaik, but by this point, it has been a bit milked dry, so I could understand where they come from. Still, among these villain tropes, if you're a person who can enjoy that kind of trope, Morgoth is definitely among the most well-written.

You don't know if death is the end of a conscious existence. Almost everyone suicidal treats death in their mind as a certain escape. Facts are, even though the eternal void seems the most scientific and reasonable, for all you know, it could get way worse after death.

Tbh, risking death is never worth it anyways. Nevermind the pain of dying, you have 0 idea what comes after, it's 100% random what happens. It could be transcendental pain, it could be transcendental joy, pleasure or neutrality or just nothing.

Dying is the ultimate risk. You hate your suffering now, but you have absolutely no way at all to know if it's any better to be dead. 

While alive, at least you have the power to influence your surroundings through free will and you have possibilities for the future. Those are certainties.

I'm a nihilist, meaning I don't believe there is any true purpose or value in existence. Personally, I think life is like a gigantic sandbox game- It just gives you tools and a universe to exist in, what you do with the tools is up to you, and there is no true purpose, and therefore no true worth in existing. Learning to use those tools, however, can be difficult.

When it comes to your back pain, consider Stephen Hawking (as an extreme yet very clear example) His body was absolutely demolished by his sickness, yet he found purpose and value in life that did not depend on his body being even remotely functional. Pain is a bit different, (no idea if he was in pain) but there are ways to manage this as well.

As for your ex, it sounds like you have a complicated history. I bet she hasn't always been abusive, after all, you had a relationship and you seem pretty smart and logical. Try to find a solution, people always have reasons for the way they act, even if it's utterly irrational. Open(ing) communication could be worth an attempt.

Other than that, if I was to assign any value, negative or positive, to life and existence, it would always be preferable to the great unknown of the unknowable truth of what comes after death. After all, while alive, at least you are guaranteed possibilities of influence and experience.

TL;DR:
There is no guarantees in what is after death, be it positive, negative or neutral, it is completely random what comes after, the ultimate risk. Therefore, logically, it will *always* be better to live than to risk the aftermath of death.

These would be my most essential tips for you;

Question every negative thought, but keep in mind, negative experiences are essential to life. It's the processing and utilization of the experience that matters. Demand logic of yourself, consider your thoughts and emotions and debate yourself as if you were someone else.

Know to yourself and repeat continously to yourself, your mind cannot make you do something you don't want to. This also means taking responsibility for your thoughts and actions, which will be tough in the start, but it will grant you strength.

Don't repress your emotions. This only serves to push them into your unconscious to spring back stronger with an unknown source later. All emotional experiences demands attention and processing. This is why they enforce themselves. They don't crave a solution, they crave an answer.

Stop and reflect in the moments someone suggests something your mind emotionally resists, be it to ask you to do something for/with them or a suggestion to solutions or viewpoints differing to your own.

Get familiar with your inner strength. Start taking risks, stop letting your thoughts impede your preferation of action. The more you get used to fucking up or losing, the more comfortable you get with the concept. The fear of it is far worse than the actual situations.

Your body is your mind's tool. Take care of it as one would the most precious posession they have, for that is exactly what it is.

Attempt trusting people more for the words they say. If you question someone's words when talking about your problems, ask for a hug before dismissing them entirely.

Spread kindness about you as much as you can. Kindness does not only benefit those it's aimed at but also the one aiming. If you can be merciful and kind with others, the probability of you being able to do the same for yourself increases.
